front: Define the G-spread, I-spread and Z-spread of a fixed-coupon bond. Why can the Z-spread differ materially from a yield-based spread?
back:
G-spread: YTM minus the interpolated government yield at the same maturity.
I-spread: YTM minus the interpolated swap rate at the same maturity.
Z-spread: the constant spread \(z\) added to every point of the benchmark zero curve such that \(\sum_i CF_i \, DF(t_i)\, e^{-z t_i} = \) dirty price (continuous compounding shown).
Yield-based spreads discount every cash flow at one rate (the YTM) and compare with a single point on the curve, so they implicitly assume a flat curve and re-investment at the YTM. On a sloped or humped curve the Z-spread is the correct constant spread because each cash flow is discounted off its own zero rate.
Interviewer follow-up: Which measure should a swap-hedged book use? The I-spread still uses a yield; the ASW or the Z-spread over the swap curve is the cleaner measure.

front: The Z-spread is the constant spread added to the {{c1::zero curve}} such that the discounted cash flows equal the {{c2::dirty price}}.
back: For an option-free bond the Z-spread is the spread the investor earns over the risk-free zero curve, cash flow by cash flow. For a callable or putable bond the Z-spread mixes credit spread with option value (see the OAS card).

front: Derive the approximate par-par asset swap spread (ASW) of a bond priced at \(P\) (per 100 par), annual coupon \(c\), against a par swap rate \(s\) with annuity \(A=\sum_i \tau_i DF_i\). Why does a discount bond have a higher ASW than \((c-s)\)?
back:
Par-par ASW is the spread that makes the asset swap worth zero at inception. The buyer pays \(P\) upfront, receives the bond coupons and par at maturity, and in exchange pays fixed \(s\) on the swap leg and receives floating plus ASW.
Equating the present values gives the approximation
\[ ASW \approx (c-s) + \frac{100-P}{A} \] The second term amortises the price gap to par over the life of the bond. A discount bond (\(P<100\)) therefore has an ASW above \(c-s\), and a premium bond has one below it.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is ASW not the same as the Z-spread? Because the floating leg is referenced to RFR (SOFR, SONIA, ESTR) and the spread is quoted over the swap curve, so ASW carries the swap-spread basis on top of the credit spread.

front: Why is the Z-spread of a callable bond larger than its OAS? What is the sign relationship for a putable bond?
back:
Z-spread \(\approx\) OAS + option cost, where the option cost is the value of the embedded option measured in spread terms.
A callable bond gives the issuer a call, so the investor is short the call. The investor's option cost is positive, so the Z-spread overstates the compensation for credit and liquidity risk and the OAS is smaller.
A putable bond is the reverse: the investor holds a put, so the option value is positive for the investor, the option cost is negative, and the Z-spread is below the OAS.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does effective duration of a callable bond fall when rates fall? Negative convexity: the call caps the price as yields drop and the issuer refinances.

front: Define spread duration and derive the CS01 of a bond. Mental-math example: $10m face, price 98, spread duration 6.
back:
Spread duration \(SD = -\frac{1}{P}\frac{\partial P}{\partial s}\), the percentage price sensitivity to a parallel change in the spread \(s\).
CS01 (dollar change per 1bp of spread widening) is \(CS01 = -\frac{\partial P}{\partial s}\times 0.0001 = P\cdot SD \cdot 0.0001\) per unit of face.
Example: \(10{,}000{,}000 \times 0.98 \times 6 \times 0.0001 \approx \$5{,}880\) per bp. For a bullet bond the spread duration is close to the modified duration measured on the Z-spread-discounted cash flows.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the spread duration of a floating-rate note small? Its coupons reset to the RFR, so the spread is only exposed until the next reset date, and spread duration is roughly the time to next reset.

front: CS01 of a bond equals {{c1::price × spread duration × 1bp}} per unit of face; for $10m, price 98 and spread duration 6 this is {{c2::≈ $5,880 per bp}}.
back: Use per-unit-face arithmetic and scale. The same formula gives the CDS CS01 when the price term is replaced by the risky annuity RPV01.

front: Define DTS (duration times spread) for a credit bond. Why do portfolio managers hedge DTS rather than spread duration alone?
back:
\(DTS = SD \times s\). It is roughly spread duration weighted by the spread level, so it proxies the spread-driven exposure to expected default loss rather than pure price sensitivity.
Two bonds with the same CS01 and different spreads have different DTS. The high-spread bond has more DTS, so a portfolio matched on DTS is matched on the spread-based risk premium exposure rather than the raw price sensitivity.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is DTS exposure not linear for a bond near distress? As spreads widen, the spread-level term grows, so DTS rises convexly and a hedge set on today's DTS drifts quickly.

front: A bond is priced at 95 (per 100 par) with a recovery assumption of 40. You are long the bond. What is its jump-to-default (JTD) loss, and why is it not simply notional times \((1-R)\)?
back:
JTD = market value minus recovery value: \(JTD = P - R \times 100 = 95 - 40 = 55\) per 100 par.
Notional times \((1-R)\) gives the loss measured against par. The bond is marked at 95, so the loss that actually hits the position is measured against its current market value. The gap of 5 points is the price already paid for, which disappears on default.
Interviewer follow-up: How does accrued interest enter? It is paid or recovered as part of the claim, so it is usually excluded from the MV-based JTD in a first pass.

front: A protection buyer holds $10m notional of single-name CDS with recovery 40%, and the position has a mark-to-market gain of $300k. What is its jump-to-default P&L?
back:
On default the buyer receives \((1-R)N = 0.6 \times 10\text{m} = \$6.0\text{m}\).
The existing MTM of $300k is already in the book, so the incremental jump gain is \(JTD_{buyer} = (1-R)N - MTM = 6.0 - 0.3 = \$5.7\text{m}\).
For the protection seller the sign flips: \(JTD_{seller} = -(1-R)N + MTM\).
Interviewer follow-up: Why does the MTM matter for JTD on CDS but not for a bond measured against par? The CDS settles at a fixed payout, so the existing mark is the only offset; a bond's JTD is measured against its own market value already, as in the previous card.

front: Write the premium leg and protection leg of a single-name CDS and derive the par spread. Assume a deterministic discount factor \(DF(t)\), survival \(Q(t)\), and recovery \(R\).
back:
Premium leg: \(S\sum_i \tau_i\, DF(t_i)\, Q(t_i)\) plus an accrual-on-default term, where \(\tau_i\) are accrual fractions. The accrual-on-default term is usually approximated as half a period of premium on the default-date distribution.
Protection leg: \((1-R)\sum_i DF(t_{i})\,[Q(t_{i-1})-Q(t_i)]\) in discrete form, or \((1-R)\int DF(t)\,dQ(t)\) in continuous form.
The par spread sets the two legs equal:
\[ S^{*} = \frac{(1-R)\sum_i DF(t_i)\,[Q(t_{i-1})-Q(t_i)]}{\sum_i \tau_i DF(t_i) Q(t_i)} \] The denominator is the risky annuity, RPV01.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does the premium leg need the accrual-on-default term? A default part-way through a period means the buyer owes the accrued premium, and the cost is not zero.

front: How are single-name CDS quoted and paid? Use a 5y IG name with par spread 80bp, standard coupon 100bp and RPV01 of 4.6. Who pays what upfront, and what about HY names?
back:
Single-name IG CDS trade with a fixed standard coupon (100bp in the North American convention) and a quoted par spread. The protection buyer pays the coupon, and the difference is settled with an upfront payment.
Upfront \(\approx (c - S^{*})\times RPV01 = (100-80)\text{bp} \times 4.6 = 0.92\) points of notional. The buyer pays 100bp but the market is 80bp, so the buyer overpays and receives 0.92 points from the seller. Accrued premium since the last coupon date is added on top.
HY names trade with a 500bp coupon, and the quote is points upfront plus the 500bp running premium.
Interviewer follow-up: Who receives the upfront if the par spread is above the coupon? The protection seller receives it, because the buyer is underpaying.

front: State the credit-triangle approximation. A 5y CDS trades at 300bp and recovery is 40%. What is the implied flat hazard rate and the approximate 5-year default probability?
back:
With a flat hazard rate \(\lambda\), the premium leg per unit time is \(S\) and the expected loss per unit time is \(\lambda(1-R)\). Equating them gives the credit triangle:
\[ S \approx \lambda (1-R) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lambda \approx \frac{S}{1-R} \] Here \(\lambda = 0.03/0.6 = 5.0\%\). The 5-year cumulative default probability is \(1-e^{-5\times0.05} = 1-e^{-0.25}\approx 22\%\).
Interviewer follow-up: When does the triangle break down? When spreads are large relative to \(1-R\), or when the rate level matters, so the risky annuity and discounting need the full model.

front: Under the credit-triangle approximation the hazard rate is \(\lambda \approx\) {{c1::\(S/(1-R)\)}}; for a 5y spread of 300bp and R = 40% this gives \(\lambda \approx\) {{c2::5%}}.
back: Each 1bp of spread is about \(1/(1-R)\) bp of hazard. This is the intuition used in mental-math conversions between spreads and PD.

front: Derive the risky annuity RPV01 under a flat hazard rate \(\lambda\) and rate \(r\). Give a mental approximation for a 5y CDS at 100bp with R = 40%.
back:
Ignoring accrual-on-default, \(RPV01 \approx \int_0^T e^{-(r+\lambda)t}\,dt = \frac{1-e^{-(r+\lambda)T}}{r+\lambda}\).
With \(\lambda = 0.01/0.6 \approx 1.67\%\) and \(r=0\), \(RPV01 \approx T - \lambda T^2/2 = 5 - 0.21 \approx 4.8\).
RPV01 is always below the risk-free annuity because each premium payment is discounted by survival as well as by the rate.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does RPV01 fall as spreads widen? Higher \(\lambda\) lowers survival, so fewer premium payments are expected, and the premium's present value drops.

front: Describe the ISDA Standard CDS Model used to convert quoted CDS spreads into hazard rates and prices. What does "flat hazard rate" mean in that context and why is it used?
back:
The ISDA model bootstraps a survival curve from quoted par spreads, using the ISDA discount curve and standard conventions (quarterly premium, accrual-on-default, standard payment dates, and the IMM maturities). Within each segment it assumes a constant (flat) hazard rate, which makes the survival curve piecewise exponential.
Flat hazard rates make the bootstrap closed-form per segment and let a single quoted spread map to a single hazard. This ties the spread to a survival probability in a way that is consistent across tenors and reproduces the quoted spreads exactly.
Upfront quotes are converted using the same survival curve and the standard coupon.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does a flat hazard curve not match the real term structure? It matches market quotes by construction, but the implied forward hazards jump at each tenor point, so forward-starting CDS priced off it can be unstable.

front: Define the CDS-bond basis. The bond ASW is 150bp and the 5y CDS is 120bp. Describe the trade and explain why it persists.
back:
Basis = CDS spread minus cash spread (ASW or Z-spread). Here \(120-150 = -30\)bp, a negative basis.
Trade: buy the bond at a 150bp asset swap spread and buy protection at 120bp. The position locks in about 30bp of spread per year, less the funding cost of the bond above the RFR.
Persistence comes from frictions: funding costs above the reference rate (repo or unsecured), the cheapest-to-deliver option embedded in the CDS, the cost of the protection seller's counterparty risk (CVA and capital), balance sheet and leverage limits, and the risk of a documentation or delivery mismatch.
Interviewer follow-up: What happens to the basis in a funding squeeze? Bond investors who finance at higher rates require wider spreads, which pushes the basis more negative.

front: Why does the cheapest-to-deliver option in a CDS push the CDS-bond basis positive? Give the protection buyer's payoff and what drives the option's value.
back:
The protection buyer's auction payoff is \((100 - P_{auc})\) per 100 notional, where \(P_{auc} = \min_j P_j\) over eligible deliverables. The buyer is paid for the cheapest bond in the deliverable set, not for a bond it owns.
The option's value is roughly the expected gap between the highest and lowest eligible post-default prices, weighted by default probability. Example: if eligible bonds settle at 30 and 40, the buyer receives 70 on the cheapest-bond auction versus 60 if the cheapest were 40, a 10-point option.
The seller of protection prices this into the running spread, so CDS spread > bond-implied spread and basis = CDS minus bond > 0.
Interviewer follow-up: What shrinks the option? Fewer eligible deliverables (restructuring clause, maturity limits, subordination, currency restrictions) and tighter post-default price dispersion across them.

front: A corporate bond is special in repo. Explain how this affects the bond's cash spread and the CDS-bond basis.
back:
Specialness means the bond is in strong demand to borrow for shorting, so the lender of the bond accepts a lower repo rate. Holders of the bond can finance cheaply, and the bond price is pushed up relative to the curve.
A higher bond price lowers the bond's yield spread, so the cash spread tightens while the CDS spread is unchanged. The basis (CDS minus cash) therefore moves positive.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the rates-based carry for a short seller the opposite? The short pays the special rate on the bond it borrows, so it is cheaper to be short when the bond is special.

front: Par-par asset swap spread versus zero-volatility spread for a callable bond: what does each measure, which way does the embedded call bias each, and which measure do you compare with a CDS?
back:
Par-par ASW is the constant spread over the floating leg that makes the bond's contractual cash flows, swapped against the floating index at par, worth par. It takes the cash flows as given and does not model optionality.
Zero-volatility spread is the constant spread over the zero curve that prices the bond with the embedded option valued with no rate volatility, so the call is exercised only along the deterministic path.
For a callable bond both measures include the option cost in the spread: the investor is short the call, the price is lower, and the spread is wider than the credit-only spread. Par-par and zero-vol therefore overstate the credit compensation. Option-adjusted spread removes the option cost, and for a putable bond the bias has the opposite sign.
A CDS has no embedded call, so compare the CDS with OAS. The gap between a non-OAS measure and OAS approximates the option cost in spread terms.
Interviewer follow-up: For a make-whole call far out of the money, which measure? All three converge, so the choice barely matters; it matters for a call that is near the money.

front: List the 2014 ISDA credit events relevant to corporate and sovereign reference entities. Which apply only to some entity types?
back:
Bankruptcy, Failure to Pay (subject to a grace period and a default threshold), Obligation Acceleration, Obligation Default, Repudiation or Moratorium, Restructuring (only if the contract includes a restructuring clause), and Governmental Intervention.
Corporates: Bankruptcy, Failure to Pay, Obligation Acceleration, Obligation Default and Restructuring if included. Repudiation or Moratorium and Governmental Intervention are not relevant.
Sovereigns: Repudiation or Moratorium and Restructuring apply.
Financial Reference Entities: Governmental Intervention is also a credit event.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is Restructuring optional in North America but treated differently in Europe? Market practice and the choice of restructuring clause were historically regional, and the 2014 definitions preserve the clause choice rather than imposing one.

front: Compare the restructuring clauses XR14, CR14, MR14 and MM14 in the 2014 definitions. What is the main purpose of the maturity limits?
back:
ClauseRestructuring is a credit event?Limit on deliverable obligation maturity after restructuring
XR14 (no restructuring)Non/a
CR14 (full restructuring)YesNone
MR14 (modified restructuring)Yes30 months
MM14 (modified-modified restructuring)Yes60 months for bonds, 30 months for loans (check clause text)
The maturity limits exist because a restructuring can keep a long-dated bond in the deliverable set. Protection buyers would then deliver the cheapest long-dated bonds, which are hard to value. Limits constrain the delivery option.
Interviewer follow-up: Which clause is most common for North American IG? XR14 has become the norm there, and European single names trade with MR or MM conventions.

front: Under MR14, the deliverable obligations after a restructuring are limited to a residual maturity of {{c1::30 months}}; this limit reduces the {{c2::cheapest-to-deliver}} option the protection buyer holds.
back: Maturity limits are the reason the restructuring clause matters for basis and delivery. MM14 relaxes the limit for bonds, and XR14 removes restructuring as a trigger altogether.

front: What is governmental intervention as a 2014 credit event, and why does it matter for bank CDS?
back:
Governmental intervention is triggered when a government or regulator action, such as a compulsory exchange, a write-down, or a conversion, reduces the obligations of a Financial Reference Entity or a Sovereign. The trigger does not need creditor consent and is decided by the Determinations Committee.
For banks this captures bail-in and resolution risk. Bank CDS can therefore price the probability of intervention through a resolution regime, even when no default in the usual sense occurs.
Interviewer follow-up: How does it differ from a restructuring? A restructuring needs a creditor-level change with a specific mechanism. Governmental intervention is imposed by the authority, so the creditor consent test does not apply.

front: Describe the CDS credit-event auction protocol and explain how the final price sets the recovery. Why is open interest netted?
back:
After a credit event is determined, a CDS auction runs. Dealers submit an initial market midpoint quote, physical settlement requests are collected, and the net open interest is calculated. Bidders then submit prices and the Final Price is set.
Cash settlement pays the protection buyer approximately \(N\times(1-\text{Final Price})\), adjusted for the coupon and accrued premium conventions. The Final Price is effectively the market recovery of the auctioned bonds.
Netting open interest reduces the number of bonds that have to be physically delivered, because only the net imbalance has to be filled.
Interviewer follow-up: Why can the final price differ from the recovery on the bonds? Auction prices reflect deliverable bonds and supply-demand, and they can differ from the eventual workout recovery.

front: What is the role of ISDA Determinations Committees and how do they treat succession events?
back:
Regional Determinations Committees (DCs) are composed of dealers and buy-side members who vote on whether a credit event has occurred, whether an auction should be held, and what the successor is. Decisions require a supermajority.
A succession event (merger, spin-off, reorganisation) can split a reference entity into successors. The DC determines the successor(s), and the CDS can be reallocated to them, so the contract may reference a different legal entity afterwards.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does succession matter for index trades? Index constituents can change after successions, which changes the index's composition and its roll behaviour.

front: After a succession event, what does the 2014 definitions concept of a "Narrowed Reference Obligation" do, and why is it needed?
back:
After a succession the successor may have obligations whose ranking, currency or maturity differ from the original reference obligation. Without a narrowing mechanism the CDS could end up referencing a broader pool than the one the protection was written on.
The Narrowed Reference Obligation concept restricts the CDS to a narrower obligation of the successor, so that the contract's exposure does not expand after the succession. The exact mechanics are defined in the clause text, so verify the operative wording in the 2014 Definitions before relying on it in an interview answer.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is this a basis risk? Two CDS on the same name can then reference different obligations after succession, so the hedge and the trade can diverge.

front: Standard composition and coupons of the four main CDS indices: iTraxx Main, iTraxx Crossover, CDX IG and CDX HY. Which ones use a 500bp coupon?
back:
iTraxx Main (European IG): 125 names, 5y, 100bp coupon.
iTraxx Crossover (European sub-IG): 75 names, 5y, 500bp coupon.
CDX IG (North American IG): 125 names, 5y, 100bp coupon.
CDX HY (North American HY): 100 names, 5y, 500bp coupon.
The HY-style indices (Crossover and CDX HY) are quoted as points upfront plus the 500bp running premium.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the composition fixed at each roll? It keeps the index a fixed portfolio for the series life, with defaults handled through the index factor rather than by rebalancing.

front: CDS index series roll semi-annually on the IMM dates {{c1::20 March and 20 September}}; a rolled series is the new {{c2::on-the-run}} series.
back: The on-the-run series is the most liquid series. Off-the-run series still trade but with declining liquidity and shorter residual maturity.

front: A protection buyer holds 10m of the old 5y index series (4.5y remaining, market 60bp) and rolls to the new on-the-run series (5y at 65bp, RPV01 about 4.4). What does the roll trade do economically, and what is its PV cost?
back:
The roll closes the old position at its market spread and opens the same-direction position in the new series. Exposure is stated in RPV01-weighted CS01, not face.
PV cost of rolling a protection buyer's position \(\approx (s_{new} - s_{old}) \times RPV01_{new} \times N = 5\text{bp} \times 4.4 \times 10\text{m} \approx \$22\text{k}\). This ignores the realised mark on the old contract, which settles at its market level.
Economic content: (i) the extra 0.5 years of tenor, so the curve slope is paid; (ii) constituent changes and defaults since the last roll; (iii) liquidity, because the old series trades less and its market spread can differ from intrinsic.
Interviewer follow-up: Why not hold the old series? Shorter tenor and thinner liquidity make its hedge harder to execute at quoted prices, and dealer inventory and quotes migrate to the new series at roll.

front: A 125-name equal-weight index has R = 40% and one name defaults. Compute the new index factor and the loss to the protection seller as a fraction of the original notional.
back:
Index factor: \(124/125 = 0.992\), so the index notional and coupons now run on 99.2% of the original notional.
Each name is weighted \(1/125 = 0.8\%\). The defaulted name pays \((1-R)\times 0.8\% = 0.6 \times 0.8\% = 0.48\%\) of the original notional to the protection buyer, paid by the seller.
The defaulted name is removed from the index, and the remaining 124 names continue. The auction on the defaulted name settles the single-name leg.
Interviewer follow-up: Who gets the loss, and why is it smaller than the index spread times one year? The loss is one-off and equals the defaulted name's weighted LGD; the coupon stream on it stops.

front: After one default in a 125-name equal-weight index the index factor becomes {{c1::124/125 ≈ 0.992}}, and the protection seller pays {{c2::(1−R)/125}} of the original notional, which is {{c3::0.48%}} at R = 40%.
back: The index factor scales future coupons and spread accruals. The loss uses the per-name weight, not the single-name spread.

front: Define index-intrinsic basis. CDX IG trades at 65bp and the constituents imply an intrinsic spread of 58bp. What trade captures the convergence and what is its carry?
back:
Index-intrinsic basis = index spread minus the weighted-average constituent spread (the intrinsic spread), adjusted for upfronts and coupon mismatches.
The index is 7bp wide. Buy index protection at 65bp and sell protection on the constituents with a weighted spread of 58bp. The position pays 7bp of net carry per year while the basis is open, and profits as the index tightens to intrinsic.
Interviewer follow-up: What causes persistent basis? Liquidity of the index relative to single names, dealer hedging demand, skew, and the costs of running many single-name positions across the constituents.

front: In a stress the CDX-style index trades 8bp wide to its intrinsic spread. Which side is the basis trader on, what is the carry, and what is the MTM if the basis widens a further 5bp on 10m with RPV01 about 4.5?
back:
Index above intrinsic: sell index protection (receive the wide index spread) and buy constituent protection (pay the narrower intrinsic). Carry is about +8bp on index notional. The position is spread-neutral but short the basis.
Further 5bp basis widening: loss on the sold index is about \(10\text{m}\times 4.5\times 5\text{bp} = \$22.5\text{k}\) if the constituents do not move with it. Convergence requires the names to widen relative to the index, so the trade is exposed to the premium of the index, not just the spread level.
Why the index is wide: hedgers concentrate demand in the liquid index; dealers' capacity to sell index protection is limited by balance sheet and risk limits; and single-name protection is harder to source in size and lags.
Interviewer follow-up: Is a wide index a buy? Only if the trader can fund the position through the widening, since the basis can overshoot before it converges.

front: Write the conditional default probability in a one-factor Gaussian copula and explain the role of the correlation parameter \(\rho\).
back:
Latent variables: \(X_i = \sqrt{\rho}\,M + \sqrt{1-\rho}\,\varepsilon_i\), with \(M\) and \(\varepsilon_i\) independent standard normals. Name \(i\) defaults when \(X_i < \Phi^{-1}(p)\), where \(p\) is the unconditional default probability.
Conditional on the common factor \(M\), defaults are independent with probability
\[ p(M) = \Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(p) - \sqrt{\rho}\,M}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right) \] Tranche expected loss is obtained by integrating over \(M\). \(\rho=0\) gives independent defaults, and \(\rho\to1\) gives all names defaulting together.
Interviewer follow-up: What does this model miss? It has no tail dependence in the limit and a single correlation for all names, which is why base correlation is used.

front: What is base correlation and why is it used instead of a single implied correlation per tranche?
back:
Base correlation for a detachment point \(K\) is the correlation \(\rho_K\) that reprices the equity tranche \([0,K]\) with the one-factor Gaussian copula. Each detachment point then has its own base correlation.
Quoting by base correlation gives a single consistent correlation curve that reprices all the quoted tranches. A single implied correlation per tranche cannot reprice the whole capital structure consistently, because a [A,B] tranche's implied correlation depends on the other tranches.
Non-equity tranches are priced from the base correlation curve by difference: \([A,B]\) = \([0,B]\) minus \([0,A]\).
Interviewer follow-up: Why can base correlation be non-monotone in K? Model and interpolation artefacts or market skew can produce a non-monotone base correlation, which implies negative values for some tranche expected losses and must be fixed.

front: A trader hedges a 3-7% mezzanine tranche with a single correlation number. Why is that wrong, and which base correlation sensitivities does the tranche actually carry?
back:
The 3-7% tranche is long the \([0,7]\) equity tranche and short \([0,3]\) in expected loss, so its value depends on two base correlation points, \(\rho(3\%)\) and \(\rho(7\%)\). It has a two-component correlation vector, not one number.
A bump to \(\rho(7\%)\) alone changes the \([0,7]\) leg; a bump to \(\rho(3\%)\) alone changes the offset. The two can move in opposite directions, so an averaged single-correlation hedge does not neutralise the tranche.
Hedge with instruments whose correlation sensitivity sits on the same two detachments (for example the \([0,3]\) and \([0,7]\) tranches, or the adjacent senior tranche for the 7% point), solving for notionals that match both components.
Interviewer follow-up: How is a senior tranche hedged? Index delta plus base correlation vega at the detachment points it spans, which for a 15-100% tranche is concentrated near the 15% point.

front: In the one-factor Gaussian copula, a rise in correlation {{c1::lowers}} the expected loss (and the spread) of the 0–3% equity tranche and {{c2::raises}} the expected loss of the senior tranche.
back: Equity expected loss falls because defaults become bunched: most scenarios have few defaults and the tranche is rarely hit. The senior tranche gains tail weight, so it loses value for a protection seller.

front: Why is the expected loss of a 3-7% mezzanine tranche a hump in correlation, while the 0-3% equity tranche's EL falls monotonically? Use the large-pool conditional loss.
back:
Large pool with \(p=5\%\), \(R=40\%\): the pool's mean loss is \((1-R)p = 3\%\) for every \(\rho\). Correlation changes the spread of the conditional loss \(L(M)\), not its mean.
Tranche EL \(= E[\min((L-A)^+, B-A)]/(B-A)\). Equity \([0,3]\): as \(\rho\) rises, the mass moves out of the band where the equity tranche is partly hit, so its EL falls (about 74%, 54%, 40% for \(\rho = 0.1, 0.3, 0.5\)).
Mezzanine \([3,7]\): at low \(\rho\), \(L\) sits near the 3% attachment and the tranche loses little. As \(\rho\) rises, mass enters the band and EL rises (about 17.2%, 19.6%). At high \(\rho\), \(L\) is mostly 0 or above 7%, so the tranche is either untouched or fully hit, and EL falls toward \(P(L > 7\%)\), about 5% as \(\rho \to 1\). The peak sits near \(\rho \approx 0.3\) for this calibration (17.8% at 0.5).
Hedge consequence: the mezzanine's correlation sensitivity changes sign across the hump, so a book marked at \(\rho = 0.1\) is long correlation in the mezzanine and a book at \(\rho = 0.5\) is short it. Hedge with index delta plus offsetting base correlation vega on the 3% and 7% points, and recheck the sign whenever the market moves across the peak.

front: Describe a knockout payer option on a CDS index and the front-end protection (FEP) feature. What happens if a constituent defaults before expiry?
back:
A payer option gives the holder the right to buy protection on the index at a strike spread at expiry. A knockout option ceases to exist if a constituent defaults before expiry.
When a constituent defaults before expiry the option holder receives the front-end protection on the defaulted name, computed as its weighted LGD, and the option knocks out.
Value to the holder is therefore the FEP payment plus the option's residual value, if any. FEP is the expected protection on defaults before expiry, and it is part of the option's price.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does a knockout index option not simply behave like a swaption on the index spread? The default payout before expiry is paid on the option, so a pure swaption model misprices the option.

front: Why must the forward index spread used to price a knockout index option be adjusted for front-end protection?
back:
The forward index spread for an option expiring at \(T\) should be computed on the index conditional on survival of the names to \(T\). If a name defaults before \(T\), the option pays FEP and the underlying forward for the remaining notional is different.
Using the unconditional forward spread for the underlying ignores the difference between the surviving notional and the notional that the option is written on, and gives a biased option price and hedge ratio.
Interviewer follow-up: Which effect is larger, FEP or the forward basis? In wide spread regimes FEP is material, so it cannot be ignored even if the forward basis is small.

front: Build a CDS spread steepener on a single name (5y and 10y). Which protection do you buy and sell, and how do you choose notionals for carry neutrality?
back:
A spread steepener profits when the long tenor widens relative to the short tenor. Buy 10y protection and sell 5y protection.
Carry neutrality sets \(N_{10} \times S_{10} = N_5 \times S_5\), so the premiums balance per unit time. With \(S_{10}=110\)bp and \(S_5=80\)bp this gives \(N_5 = 1.375\,N_{10}\).
Interviewer follow-up: Is this trade also jump-to-default neutral? No. The buyer of 10y protection gains \((1-R)N_{10}\) on default while the seller of 5y protection loses \((1-R)N_5\), so the net JTD is \((1-R)(N_{10}-N_5) \ne 0\).

front: For a one-issuer 5s10s curve trade (5y protection at 120bp, 10y at 150bp, recovery 40%), compare the carry-neutral and JTD-neutral notionals. Give both answers and the residual book exposure under each rule.
back:
Carry-neutral (running premium, ignoring RPV01 differences): \(N_{10} s_{10} = N_5 s_5\), so \(N_{10} = (120/150)\,N_5 = 0.8\,N_5\). Book JTD = \((1-R)(N_{10} - N_5) = 0.6 \times (-0.2) N_5\). With \(N_5 = 10\text{m}\) the book is short \$1.2m of default exposure.
JTD-neutral: \(N_{10} = N_5\), so carry = \((s_5 - s_{10})N_5 = -30\text{bp}\times 10\text{m} = -\$30\text{k}\) per year.
Both rules coincide only when \(s_5 = s_{10}\). The steeper the CDS curve, the further apart they are. Carry-neutral leaves default exposure; JTD-neutral leaves negative carry and a long-10y CS01 slope exposure.
Interviewer follow-up: Which rule for a steepener in a jump-risk regime? JTD-neutral: the cost is \$30k of carry per year, against \$1.2m of default exposure that carry-neutral would leave.

front: A JTD-neutral 5s10s CDS steepener (equal notionals, same recovery) carries {{c1::negative}} carry when the 10y spread is wider than the 5y, because the 10y protection bought costs {{c2::more}} than the 5y premium received.
back: Carry is \((S_5 - S_{10}) N\) per year. A steeper curve is therefore negative carry for the steepener, which is the price of the JTD neutrality.

front: What is a recovery lock on a CDS, and what is the payoff for the protection buyer?
back:
A recovery lock fixes the recovery used in the CDS settlement at \(R_{lock}\), so that the contract pays on a locked recovery rather than the realised one.
The protection buyer's payoff is \((R_{lock} - R_{actual})\,N\) on top of the standard settlement. Their net payout is \((1-R_{lock})N\) in place of \((1-R_{actual})N\).
A buyer who locks at 40% gains if the realised recovery is below 40% and loses if it is above, so the buyer is long low recovery. The recovery lock is a pure recovery view and removes the default-recovery uncertainty from the payout.
Interviewer follow-up: Who takes the other side? A counterparty that expects recoveries above the locked level, which is short low-recovery exposure, so the lock is a recovery swap between two views.

front: With a 5y CDS at 100bp, how does the implied hazard rate change if the assumed recovery moves from 40% to 39%? Why does the sign of the change matter for a trader?
back:
Credit triangle: \(\lambda = S/(1-R)\).
At R = 40%: \(\lambda = 0.01/0.60 = 1.667\%\).
At R = 39%: \(\lambda = 0.01/0.61 = 1.639\%\).
A one point drop in the assumed recovery lowers the hazard by about 2.7bp of hazard, or about 1.6% relative. Higher recovery means each default costs less, so a fixed spread requires a higher implied default rate. Lower recovery means the reverse.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does the recovery assumption matter more for distressed names? At a high spread the \(1-R\) denominator drives most of the hazard, so small recovery changes move implied default probabilities more.

front: Construct a long dispersion trade on an equity index and state what it profits from.
back:
Long dispersion is long single-name volatility (or variance) across the constituents and short index volatility (or variance), vega-weighted so that the net exposure is to correlation.
It profits when the index moves less than its constituents, which is when realised correlation falls below the level implied by index options. Short dispersion is the reverse.
Variance-swap versions are used to hedge the vol exposure precisely.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the trade exposed in a crisis? In a macro sell-off correlations spike and dispersion collapses, which hurts a long dispersion book.

front: For N equal-weight names with equal volatility \(\sigma\) and index volatility \(\sigma_I\), the implied correlation is \(\rho = \) {{c1::\((\sigma_I^2/\sigma^2 - 1/N)/(1-1/N)\)}}; this comes from \(\sigma_I^2 = \sigma^2\,(1/N + (1-1/N)\rho)\).
back: General form for unequal weights \(w_i\) and vols \(\sigma_i\): \(\rho_{impl} = \dfrac{\sigma_I^2 - \sum_i w_i^2\sigma_i^2}{(\sum_i w_i\sigma_i)^2 - \sum_i w_i^2\sigma_i^2}\).

front: Derive the beta-adjusted index notional that hedges the market-driven spread risk of a single-name CDS position. Define the spread beta.
back:
Spread beta \(\beta = \Delta S_{name}/\Delta S_{index}\), estimated by regression of single-name spread changes on index spread changes.
Require the CS01 of the index hedge to match the index-driven part of the name's CS01: \(N_{index}\,RPV01_{index}\,\Delta S_{index} = N_{name}\,RPV01_{name}\,\beta\,\Delta S_{index}\). Solving,
\[ N_{index} = \beta\, N_{name}\,\frac{RPV01_{name}}{RPV01_{index}} \] Only the index-driven part is hedged; the residual idiosyncratic spread risk stays on.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is beta-adjusting not enough on its own? Beta is a regression estimate that is unstable, and the idiosyncratic residual dominates in event-driven names.

front: Index notional for a single-name hedge is {{c1::\(\beta \times N_{name} \times RPV01_{name}/RPV01_{index}\)}}, where β is the spread beta, and for a name with β = 2 and the same tenor it is {{c2::twice the single-name notional}}.
back: A name that moves twice as much as the index needs twice the index notional to neutralise index-driven exposure.

front: Sovereign CDS: what is redenomination risk, and how does a euro-area sovereign's exit from the euro interact with its CDS contract?
back:
Redenomination risk is the risk that a sovereign's bonds are converted into a new currency that is expected to depreciate. The contract's payout and the reference obligation then diverge, because the bond's currency changes while the CDS currency may not.
Redenomination is handled as a restructuring-type event in the credit event analysis, so it can in principle trigger a payout. Whether and how it does so depends on the clause text and the Determinations Committee, so verify the operative wording before relying on it.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is this a quanto problem? The payout is converted into the contract currency at a fixed rate while the bond is in a depreciating currency, so default and FX are linked.

front: What is a quanto CDS and what does the quanto adjustment price?
back:
A quanto CDS pays in a currency different from the currency of the reference obligation. The recovery payout is converted at a pre-set FX rate, so the protection buyer is exposed to FX at default.
The quanto adjustment prices the covariance between the reference entity's default and the FX rate. The adjustment is a spread shift that depends on the sign of that correlation, so it is not a simple FX hedge.
Interviewer follow-up: Does a quanto CDS need a separate correlation input? Yes. Without a credit-FX correlation assumption the adjustment cannot be estimated, which is why it is a model-risk item.

front: Approximate the CVA of a derivative exposure using CDS spreads. Give the formula and explain the link to the credit triangle.
back:
With exposure \(EE(t)\), discount factor \(DF(t)\), and default probability \(PD\), CVA is \((1-R)\sum_i DF(t_i)\,EE(t_i)\,\Delta PD_i\).
Using the credit triangle, \((1-R)\Delta PD_i \approx S(t_i)\,\Delta t_i\). Substituting gives
\[ CVA \approx \sum_i DF(t_i)\,EE(t_i)\,S(t_i)\,\Delta t_i \] So each CDS spread point multiplies the expected exposure at that date. This is why CDS spreads are used to hedge CVA.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is this approximation not enough for wrong-way risk? It assumes exposure and default are independent, and wrong-way risk breaks that link.

front: Define debit valuation adjustment (DVA) on a bank's derivative book. Write it in terms of the bank's own survival and expected negative exposure, and explain why a widening of the bank's own spread produces a P&L gain.
back:
DVA = \((1-R_b)\int DF(t)\,ENE(t)\,dQ_b(t)\), where \(ENE(t)\) is the expected negative exposure (value the bank owes its counterparty) and \(Q_b\) is the bank's survival. It is the CVA formula applied to the bank's own default.
When the bank's hazard rises, the probability it defaults before its liabilities mature rises, and the payments it owes are worth less. The fair value of the liability falls, so the bank books a gain roughly equal to the reduction in expected payments on its net negative book.
Controversy: the gain is largest when the bank is weakest; the bank cannot buy protection on itself, so hedges are proxies with large basis; and credit deterioration produces an accounting gain. Basel III removes DVA on derivative liabilities from CET1 (approximately; check current rules).
Interviewer follow-up: Why not hedge with the bank's own bonds? Repurchasing its own debt offsets part of the exposure but changes funding and the bank's own curve, so the hedge is partial.

front: Breakeven spread widening vs carry. A protection buyer holds a 5y CDS at 100bp with RPV01 about 4.8. What spread widening over one month offsets one month of carry?
back:
Carry of a protection buyer over one month is roughly \(-S\times\frac{1}{12} = -8.3\)bp of notional in premium terms.
Breakeven widening \(\Delta s\) satisfies \(\Delta s \times RPV01 = S/12\), so \(\Delta s \approx 8.3/4.8 \approx 1.7\)bp.
Over one month, a spread widening of more than about 1.7bp gives the protection buyer a net gain on the position, ignoring convexity and the time value of the payout.
Interviewer follow-up: What is the annual breakeven? \(S/RPV01 = 100/4.8 \approx 21\)bp per year. One month is one-twelfth of the carry, so the monthly breakeven is one-twelfth of that, about 1.7bp.

front: P&L = spread change times CS01. A protection buyer holds $25m notional of a 5y CDS with RPV01 4.8. Spreads widen 20bp. What is the approximate P&L, and what are the limitations of the approximation?
back:
CS01 \(= N\times RPV01\times 0.0001 = 25{,}000{,}000\times4.8\times0.0001 = \$12{,}000\) per bp.
P&L for the buyer \(\approx 20 \times \$12{,}000 = \$240{,}000\) gain, since spread widening benefits the protection buyer.
Limitations: the approximation is linear in the spread change. For large moves the CS01 changes because RPV01 falls as spreads widen, so the true P&L is slightly below the linear estimate for widening moves.
Interviewer follow-up: What is the sign for the seller? The seller loses $240k in the same move.

front: At RPV01 ≈ 4.8, a $10m 5y CDS has a CS01 of about {{c1::$4,800 per bp}}, so a 15bp widening moves the protection buyer's P&L by roughly {{c2::$72,000}}.
back: Scale check: \(10{,}000{,}000 \times 4.8 \times 0.0001 = 4{,}800\). Multiply by the spread change in bp. Ignore convexity for mental math.

front:
[Chain: NEG_BASIS 1/5] Context: 5y bond bought at an asset-swap spread of 150bp; 5y CDS protection bought at 120bp; basis = CDS minus bond = -30bp.
Set up the trade cash flows. What is the running carry before funding, which credit risks remain, and what is the sign of the basis?
back:
Long the bond via the asset swap receives the floating leg plus 150bp; long CDS protection pays 120bp. Net running carry is about +30bp per year on notional before funding, so the trade is long a positive carry against a negative basis.
Credit risk of the bond is largely offset by the protection, because both are exposed to the same issuer's default. What remains is (i) the basis itself (the CDS and asset swap can move apart), (ii) recovery mismatch at default (the CDS pays on the auction price, the bond pays its own realised price), (iii) counterparty risk on the protection seller, and (iv) funding.
Interviewer follow-up: Which of these risks is the trade actually paid for? The basis is the compensation; the others are costs the trader is carrying.

front:
[Chain: NEG_BASIS 2/5] Context: 5y bond bought at an asset-swap spread of 150bp; 5y CDS protection bought at 120bp; basis = CDS minus bond = -30bp.
The bond is financed in repo. How does the funding leg change the carry of the trade?
back:
Carry is approximately ASW minus CDS, minus (repo rate minus the floating index) times the funded amount, minus hedging and margin costs. The asset swap pays the floating leg flat on the risk-free rate (for a GBP bond, SONIA-based), so any difference between the repo rate on the bond and that index is a funding basis that comes straight out of the carry.
Example: repo at SONIA + 10bp on 10m gives a 10bp drag, so the 30bp basis becomes about 20bp of net carry. Special repo (bond trading tight in repo) can add carry, but specialness is itself unstable.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the negative basis not simply "arbitrage" when the carry depends on repo? Because the cash bond must be financed for the life of the trade, and haircut changes or a failed roll turn the funding leg into a forced sale.

front:
[Chain: NEG_BASIS 3/5] Context: 5y bond bought at an asset-swap spread of 150bp; 5y CDS protection bought at 120bp; basis = CDS minus bond = -30bp.
The trader owns one specific bond, but the CDS auction price is set by the cheapest deliverable obligation. What is the P&L across default as a function of the trader's own bond price?
back:
Let the trader's bond recover its own price \(P_{own}\) (per 100), and let the auction settle at \(P_{auc} = \min_j P_j\) over eligible deliverables. The CDS pays \((100 - P_{auc})\) per 100 notional; the bond delivers \(P_{own}\).
Net P&L across default per 100 notional, ignoring carry and the asset-swap unwind, is \(P_{own} + (100 - P_{auc}) - 100 = P_{own} - P_{auc}\).
If the trader's bond is itself an eligible deliverable, then \(P_{auc} \le P_{own}\) by construction, so this term is never negative: the trader holds a long option on the cheapest deliverable. Numbers: \(P_{own}=40\), \(P_{auc}=35\) gives +5 points, or +\$500k on \$10m.
If the bond is not eligible (for example a different maturity or ranking), the sign is undetermined and the mismatch becomes a genuine basis risk.
Interviewer follow-up: Does a negative basis mean the trader is paid for this option? Only partly. The CDS spread is set by the market for the cheapest-deliverable option, so a negative basis means the bond is cheap relative to a delivery-option-inclusive CDS. The trade's return is then the basis plus whatever the option is worth on default, and both can reverse in stress.

front:
[Chain: NEG_BASIS 4/5] Context: 5y bond bought at an asset-swap spread of 150bp; 5y CDS protection bought at 120bp; basis = CDS minus bond = -30bp.
Stress: the bond's asset-swap spread widens to 250bp and the CDS widens to 170bp (basis now -80bp). Bond spread duration about 4.5, CDS RPV01 about 4.4, notional 10m. What is the mark-to-market before any default, and what happens with margin?
back:
Bond MTM: \(-100\text{bp} \times 4.5 \times \$10\text{m} \times 10^{-4} = -\$450\text{k}\).
CDS protection bought, MTM: \(+50\text{bp} \times 4.4 \times \$10\text{m} \times 10^{-4} = +\$220\text{k}\).
Net mark: about -\$230k with no default. Carry earned at 30bp is \$30k per year, so the loss equals about 7.7 years of carry.
Variation margin on the CDS leg moves cash to the trader (they are the protection buyer and the spread rose) which helps funding, but the bond is funded in repo where haircuts and margin calls rise in stress. The forced-selling feedback is what turns a mark into a realised loss.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does the basis widen in stress? The bond is a funded, capital-intensive asset, so dealers and levered holders are forced to sell, while the index and CDS remain the hedging venue.

front:
[Chain: NEG_BASIS 5/5] Context: 5y bond bought at an asset-swap spread of 150bp; 5y CDS protection bought at 120bp; basis = CDS minus bond = -30bp.
Given the stress numbers from the previous card, how long must the basis trade be held and how much must it be leveraged for the arbitrage to be worth the risk?
back:
Breakeven time to recover a mark-to-market loss \(M\) from carry \(c\) per year: \(T = M/c\). Here \(M = \$230\text{k}\) and \(c = \$30\text{k}\) per year, so \(T \approx 7.7\) years on the 10m position, which is longer than the 5y tenor.
So the trade only pays if the basis converges without a forced unwind, or if the position is financed with no mark-to-market-linked margin. Leverage on a 30bp carry raises the return on equity but moves the breakeven proportionally: a 4x levered book needs the same 7.7 years on mark, but the margin calls arrive earlier.
Interviewer follow-up: What is the tail-risk hedge? Hedging the basis with the index reduces spread-direction risk, but not the basis risk, which is what the stress loss is made of.

front:
[Chain: IDX_BASIS 1/5] Context: CDX-style IG index at 65bp; intrinsic spread implied by its 125 constituents is 58bp; index basis = +7bp.
Which side of the index-versus-constituent trade captures the 7bp, and what is its running carry per 10m of index notional?
back:
Sell index protection (receive 65bp) and buy protection on the constituents with weights matched to the index (pay 58bp equivalent). Carry is +7bp on the index notional, so \(+\$7\text{k}\) per year on 10m.
Intrinsic spread is approximately the notional-weighted average of constituent par spreads when tenors and recoveries are common. It is not a simple average once constituents have different survival profiles, because the RPV01 weights and the defaulted names shift the effective weights.
Interviewer follow-up: Why is the trade sized in RPV01-matched notional and not by face? Because CS01 on each leg depends on its own spread level; equal face is not equal spread risk.

front:
[Chain: IDX_BASIS 2/5] Context: CDX-style IG index at 65bp; intrinsic spread implied by its 125 constituents is 58bp; index basis = +7bp.
A constituent defaults one day after the trade is put on. Show that the default is almost fully hedged, and what changes in the position afterwards.
back:
Short index protection: the seller pays \((1-R)/N\) of index notional on the defaulting name, with \(N = 125\), so \(0.6/125 = 0.48\%\) at \(R=40\%\). Bought constituent protection: the buyer receives \((1-R)\) times its own notional. If that notional is \(1/125\) of the index, both legs cancel exactly.
After the default, both legs amortise by 1/125: the index factor becomes 124/125, the constituent protection is gone, and the surviving hedge must be re-sized. The carry shrinks by 1/125 of its prior value. The residual mismatch is any difference in recovery between the index settlement and the constituent auction.
Interviewer follow-up: Is the trade default-neutral? Only if the recovery on the index and on the name agree; with a recovery mismatch the residual is (R_index - R_name) times the defaulted notional.

front:
[Chain: IDX_BASIS 3/5] Context: CDX-style IG index at 65bp; intrinsic spread implied by its 125 constituents is 58bp; index basis = +7bp.
The 7bp arbitrage is "free money" on paper. Why does it persist at scale? Quantify with 1bn of index notional.
back:
On 1bn index notional, 7bp is \(\$700\text{k}\) per year. The gross number is not the net number: the trade needs roughly 125 single-name legs, each with its own bid-offer and its own inventory risk.
Illustrative cost: if each leg carries a half bid-offer of about 0.5bp of running spread on its share, the average drag is around 0.5bp, leaving about 6.5bp. Add balance-sheet charges for holding 125 single-name CDS against a netted index position, and the sub-10bp basis may not clear the hurdle in normal markets. This is approximate and depends on the desk's netting and capital.
Interviewer follow-up: Why does the basis persist if the cost is small? Capacity: the arbitrage is only worth a balance sheet when it is large, and its size is limited by the constituent liquidity it needs.

front:
[Chain: IDX_BASIS 4/5] Context: CDX-style IG index at 65bp; intrinsic spread implied by its 125 constituents is 58bp; index basis = +7bp.
In a stress the basis goes from +7bp to +15bp (index wider than intrinsic). The arbitrage is short index protection. Who is pushing the index wide, and what is the MTM of the trade on 10m of index notional with RPV01 about 4.5?
back:
Index protection is the liquid, cheap venue for hedging, so clients who want to buy protection bid up the index; dealers who sell index protection demand a premium for scarce balance sheet. Single-name protection is harder to source in size, so the single-name leg does not move up as fast.
MTM on the sold index for an 8bp widening of the basis (index moving up relative to names) on 10m with RPV01 4.5: \(10\text{m} \times 4.5 \times 8\text{bp} \times 10^{-4}\) ≈ \$36k loss if the constituents do not follow. The arbitrageur is short the index exactly where the clients are buying.
Interviewer follow-up: Is a wide index always a buying opportunity? Only if the trader can fund the position through the widening; the basis can overshoot before it converges.

front:
[Chain: IDX_BASIS 5/5] Context: CDX-style IG index at 65bp; intrinsic spread implied by its 125 constituents is 58bp; index basis = +7bp.
The index is rebalanced on the next roll: one constituent is replaced, and the intrinsic spread changes. What does the trader have to re-hedge, and why does a rebalance create basis P&L that is not spread risk?
back:
The new constituent has a different spread, recovery and RPV01. The intrinsic changes by roughly \((s_{new} - s_{old})/N\) on the equal-weight basis, but the old name's CDS position is closed at its market price, which may differ from its intrinsic contribution. The gap is realised P&L on the roll, not spread risk.
Also the index series rolls to new maturity: the old series' basis and the new series' basis can differ by the roll basis (liquidity and maturity), so the trader must cross both.
Interviewer follow-up: Is the arbitrage hedged across a roll? Not perfectly; it is hedged in spread and default risk for the current series, and the roll is a separate basis trade.

front:
[Chain: BASECORR 1/5] Context: one-factor Gaussian copula calibrated to a 5y CDX-style index with market quotes on 0-3%, 0-7%, 0-15%, 0-100% tranches.
Define base correlation and explain why it is defined on equity tranches \([0,K]\) rather than on each tranche.
back:
The base correlation at detachment \(K\), \(\rho(K)\), is the single correlation in the one-factor copula that reprices the equity tranche \([0,K]\) to its market price, with the same index spread and recovery. Each \([0,K]\) tranche has a single payoff exposure, so it can be inverted for one number.
A non-equity tranche \([K_1,K_2]\) is the difference of two equity tranches, \(EL[K_1,K_2] = EL[0,K_2] - EL[0,K_1]\), so it can be priced from the base curve at two points. This is what makes the base curve the natural object.
Interviewer follow-up: Why not invert each tranche to its own implied correlation? The mezzanine tranche has no unique implied correlation in the copula: its EL is not monotone in correlation, so the inversion can have zero or two solutions (see the mezz card in this deck).

front:
[Chain: BASECORR 2/5] Context: one-factor Gaussian copula calibrated to a 5y CDX-style index with market quotes on 0-3%, 0-7%, 0-15%, 0-100% tranches.
Market base correlations usually rise with detachment (for example 25% at 3%, 40% at 7%, 60% at 15%). Why is that consistent with the copula, and what constraint must the base curve satisfy?
back:
The rising shape is the skew: senior tranches are priced as if default dependence is higher in the tail. A single-correlation copula underprices senior protection relative to the equity tranche, so the base curve compensates by pushing \(\rho(K)\) up.
No-arbitrage constraint: the expected loss of each equity tranche \(EL[0,K]\) must be non-decreasing in \(K\), and every non-equity tranche must have non-negative EL, \(EL[K_1,K_2] \ge 0\). Interpolating \(\rho(K)\) between quoted points can violate this if the curve falls too steeply between two strikes, producing a negative-priced mezzanine tranche.
Interviewer follow-up: How do you enforce it? Interpolate the expected loss curve (or the base correlation in a monotone way) and check each tranche EL is positive and the tranche sum reconciles.

front:
[Chain: BASECORR 3/5] Context: one-factor Gaussian copula calibrated to a 5y CDX-style index with market quotes on 0-3%, 0-7%, 0-15%, 0-100% tranches.
Index spread moves up by 1bp. What is the delta of the 3-7% mezzanine tranche to the index, and should base correlation be held fixed when you compute it?
back:
Delta to the index is \(\partial V_{3\text{-}7}/\partial S_I\) with the base correlations held at their quoted points, expressed as an index notional: \(N_I = \frac{\partial V_{3\text{-}7}/\partial S_I}{RPV01_I \times 1\text{bp}}\).
Two conventions exist. Sticky strike holds \(\rho(K)\) fixed at each detachment, so the index move changes only the tranche's market-implied loss. Sticky delta moves \(\rho(K)\) with the index so the implied correlation is re-based. Delta under sticky strike is the standard hedging convention in the copula; the two can differ materially for mezzanine tranches, where the tranche's sensitivity depends on where correlation sits on the hump.
Interviewer follow-up: Which convention would a risk manager use for a hedge over a 1bp move? Sticky strike is the default for small moves; sticky delta is the check for stress.

front:
[Chain: BASECORR 4/5] Context: one-factor Gaussian copula calibrated to a 5y CDX-style index with market quotes on 0-3%, 0-7%, 0-15%, 0-100% tranches.
Why does one base correlation hedge (for example one index tranche sold against another) not neutralise the book's correlation risk?
back:
Each point on the base curve is an independent risk factor, so the book's correlation exposure is a vector \((\partial V/\partial \rho(K_1), \dots, \partial V/\partial \rho(K_n))\) — a Corr01 by detachment. A single hedge instrument neutralises one component.
To hedge the vector, choose n instruments whose Corr01 vectors are independent, e.g. long equity tranche against short senior tranche, and solve the linear system for the notionals so the total Corr01 at each detachment is zero. Two instruments hedge two components; they leave the curve shape (slope and curvature in \(K\)) exposed.
Interviewer follow-up: Why do desks still say "correlation hedged" with a long-short equity-senior book? Because it is hedged at the two detachments that carry most of the vega; the residual is the mezzanine slope risk.

front:
[Chain: BASECORR 5/5] Context: one-factor Gaussian copula calibrated to a 5y CDX-style index with market quotes on 0-3%, 0-7%, 0-15%, 0-100% tranches.
One constituent defaults (125 names, recovery 40%). What happens to the equity tranche 0-3% and why does a correlation hedge built on that tranche move?
back:
The default removes \((1-R)/125 = 0.48\%\) of index notional as loss. Against a 3% equity tranche, that is \(0.48/3 = 16\%\) of its notional consumed in one name.
After the default, the equity tranche's remaining notional is 2.52% of the original index and its attachment in terms of surviving names shifts. The base correlation curve is re-calibrated to the new index factor, so the \(\rho(3\%)\) point can move even though no spread moved. The correlation hedge therefore carries a jump-to-default component that is not in the Corr01 vector.
Interviewer follow-up: How do you measure it? Compute the book's P&L with one name removed and the base curve re-calibrated to the reduced index, not a shifted curve.

front: Derivation: A 5y CDS has flat hazard \(\lambda\), flat continuously compounded rate \(r\), recovery \(R\), and premium accrued on default. Derive the par spread. Compare quarterly discrete premiums with the continuous limit.
back:
Step 1 (premium leg per unit spread). With payments at \(t_i\) and survival \(Q(t)=e^{-\lambda t}\), the scheduled premium is \(\sum_i \tau\, DF(t_i) Q(t_i)\). Premium accrued on default in period \(i\) is approximately \(\frac{\tau}{2} DF(t_{mid}) (Q(t_{i-1}) - Q(t_i))\), i.e. default assumed at mid-period.
Step 2 (protection leg). \((1-R)\sum_i DF(t_{mid}) (Q(t_{i-1}) - Q(t_i))\), with settlement at default.
Step 3 (par). Par spread \(s = (1-R)\sum DF(Q_{i-1}-Q_i) \,/\, \sum \tau DF Q_i + \text{accrued term}\).
Step 4 (continuous limit). With continuous premium and full accrual, the premium annuity is \(\int_0^T DF(t)Q(t)\,dt = (1-e^{-(r+\lambda)T})/(r+\lambda)\), and the protection is \((1-R)\lambda\int_0^T e^{-(r+\lambda)t}dt\). The ratio is \(s = (1-R)\lambda\) exactly, independent of \(r\).
Numbers (5y, \(\lambda=5\%\), \(R=40\%\), \(r=3\%\)): discrete quarterly without accrual 303.0bp; with accrued on default 301.1bp; continuous limit 300.0bp. RPV01 discrete with accrual 4.106 versus continuous 4.121.
Where it breaks: the identity \(s=\lambda(1-R)\) needs flat hazard and continuous premium. Piecewise-flat hazard (what the market curve bootstraps to) makes the par an average of the segment spreads weighted by the annuity, not the segment hazard times loss.

front: Derivation: Under the ISDA standard CDS model, write the upfront of a single-name CDS with par spread \(s\) and standard coupon \(c\). Who pays the upfront when \(s > c\)? Check the sign at 500bp.
back:
Step 1 (model). The ISDA standard model bootstraps a piecewise-flat hazard curve from the par spreads of the standard tenors, using ACT/360 and the IMM schedule, with a common discount curve. The model is not a closed form: the risky annuity \(RPV01\) is computed on the bootstrapped curve.
Step 2 (value to the protection buyer). \(V_{buyer} = PV_{prot} - PV_{prem}(c) = s\cdot RPV01 - c\cdot RPV01 = (s-c)\,RPV01\) per unit notional (using \(PV_{prot}=s\,RPV01\) at fair spread).
Step 3 (upfront). The buyer pays \(U = (s-c)\,RPV01\) for the contract to be fair at coupon \(c\), plus the accrued premium from the last coupon date (ACT/360), which is cash and not part of \(U\).
Numbers. \(s=300\)bp, \(c=100\)bp, \(RPV01 \approx 4.106\) (flat \(\lambda=5\%\), \(R=40\%\), 5y): \(U = 0.02 \times 4.106 = 8.21\) points, or \$821k on \$10m. At \(c=500\)bp the sign flips: \(U = -8.21\) points, so the seller pays the buyer.
Where it breaks: \(RPV01\) depends on the bootstrapped curve, which is itself calibrated to the quoted spread, so a change in the quoted convention (for example moving from par to upfront quotes) changes the hazard as well as the value. The linear formula is exact given \(RPV01\); the approximation risk sits in the curve, not the formula.

front: Derivation: Derive the forward par spread of a CDS starting at \(T_1\) and maturing at \(T_2\), under flat hazard \(\lambda\), flat rate \(r\), recovery \(R\), continuous premium. What does your result say about the shape of the forward curve?
back:
Step 1. Let \(\Delta = e^{-(r+\lambda)T_1} - e^{-(r+\lambda)T_2}\). Forward protection leg: \((1-R)\lambda\int_{T_1}^{T_2} e^{-(r+\lambda)t}dt = (1-R)\lambda\,\Delta/(r+\lambda)\).
Step 2. Forward premium annuity: \(\int_{T_1}^{T_2} e^{-(r+\lambda)t}dt = \Delta/(r+\lambda)\) (survival and discounting combined into one exponent under flat hazard).
Step 3. Forward spread = ratio = \((1-R)\lambda\), independent of \(T_1\), \(T_2\) and \(r\).
Consequence. Under flat hazard the forward par curve is flat at \(\lambda(1-R)\) and equals the spot par spread. Any slope in the forward curve is therefore evidence of a term structure in hazard, not of the rate curve.
Where it breaks: the flat-forward result needs the same hazard in \([T_1,T_2]\) and the forward premium to be continuous; discrete premiums and the accrual correction add a few tenths of a basis point. With a time-varying hazard the forward equals the hazard-weighted average over the window, which is why forwards are used to read term structure.

front: Derivation: A knockout payer option on a CDS index with \(N\) equal-weight names, common hazard \(\lambda\), recovery \(R\), flat rate \(r\), expiry \(T\). Derive the front-end protection (FEP) value. Why must it be added to the Black value of the surviving index, and what does the decomposition look like for a one-month expiry?
back:
Convention. Under a knockout, the first default among the \(N\) names extinguishes the option and the holder receives the protection on the defaulted name, \((1-R)/N\) of index notional, paid at default. Otherwise the option pays its Black payoff at \(T\).
Step 1 (first-default intensity). With independent names of hazard \(\lambda\), the first default has intensity \(N\lambda\).
Step 2 (FEP value). \(FEP = \int_0^T \frac{1-R}{N}\,N\lambda\,e^{-N\lambda t}\,e^{-rt}\,dt = \frac{(1-R)\lambda}{N\lambda + r}\left(1-e^{-(N\lambda+r)T}\right)\).
Step 3 (decomposition). Value = FEP + \(P(\text{no default before }T)\times\) (Black value on the surviving index), with \(P = e^{-N\lambda T}\).
Numbers. \(N=125\), \(\lambda=5\%\), \(R=40\%\), \(r=3\%\). For \(T=1\)m: FEP ≈ 0.195% of index notional and \(P(\text{no default}) \approx 0.59\). For \(T=1\)y: FEP ≈ 0.477% (≈ \((1-R)/N = 0.48\%\)) and \(P \approx 0.002\), so the option is almost entirely FEP.
Where it breaks: the Black term must use the forward spread of survivors, not the full index forward, otherwise the defaulted names are double counted. Heterogeneous hazards, default correlation and the exact knockout wording in a given contract change the convention; this derivation assumes independent homogeneous names.

front: Derivation: Derive the expected loss of a tranche \([A,B]\) in the large homogeneous pool limit of the one-factor Gaussian copula with pool default probability \(p\), correlation \(\rho\), recovery \(R\). Evaluate for \(p=5\%\), \(R=40\%\), \(\rho=0.3\).
back:
Step 1 (conditional default). Given market factor \(M\sim N(0,1)\), each name defaults with \(p(M)=\Phi\big((\Phi^{-1}(p)-\sqrt{\rho}\,M)/\sqrt{1-\rho}\big)\), independently.
Step 2 (LHP). With infinitely many names, the pool loss given \(M\) is deterministic: \(L(M) = (1-R)\,p(M)\).
Step 3 (tranche loss). Tranche loss is \(\min\big((L-A)^+, B-A\big)\); the expected loss as a fraction of tranche notional is \(EL[A,B] = \frac{1}{B-A}\,E_M\big[\min((L(M)-A)^+,\,B-A)\big]\).
Numbers. Unconditional pool EL is \((1-R)p = 3.0\%\). Results: 0-3% tranche 54.1% of notional; 3-7% 19.6%; 7-15% 5.8%; 15-100% 0.15% (quadrature). Check: \(0.03(54.1)+0.04(19.6)+0.08(5.8)+0.85(0.15)\%\) = 3.00% of index.
Where it breaks: at \(N=125\) granularity noise matters for the equity tranche; the LHP ignores it. The Gaussian copula's thin tails and a single \(\rho\) mis-price senior and mezzanine tranches, which is why base correlation is needed.

front: Derivation: Derive the jump-to-default P&L of a single-name CDS position with notional \(N\), recovery \(R\) and mark-to-market \(V\) to the holder. Apply it to a 5s10s steepener on one issuer where the 10y protection bought has moved from 150bp to 160bp.
back:
Step 1. At default, a protection buyer receives \(N(1-R)\) and the contract terminates. The mark \(V\) that existed just before default is lost.
Step 2. P&L at default \(= N(1-R) - V\). This is the JTD. For a fresh at-par trade \(V = 0\) and JTD \(= N(1-R)\). For a seller of protection the sign of both terms flips.
Step 3 (MTM for a buyer). \(V = (s_{mkt} - c)\,RPV01\,N\).
Step 4 (numbers). \(RPV01_{10y} \approx 7.69\) at 150bp, \(R=40\%\). Spread moves 150 to 160bp, so \(V_{10} = (0.0160-0.0150)\times 7.69 \times 10\text{m} = \$76.9\text{k}\). JTD of the 10y bought leg = \(6.00\text{m} - 0.077\text{m} = 5.92\text{m}\). If the 5y sold leg is at par (\(V=0\)) its JTD is \(-6.00\text{m}\). Book JTD = \(-\$77\text{k}\), not zero.
Where it breaks: the equal-notional JTD neutrality holds only at inception. Any move in the legs makes \(V\neq 0\) and shifts the book's JTD. Different recoveries on the legs (for example a sub-debt versus senior contract) break the equal-notional rule even at inception.

front: Case study: A 5y CDS on a distressed name quotes 300bp running; the standard coupon is 100bp. Convert to points upfront. Use RPV01 about 4.11 (flat \(\lambda=5\%\), \(R=40\%\)). Check the answer with the opposite coupon.
back:
Step 1. Spread-coupon gap: \(s - c = 3.00\% - 1.00\% = 2.00\%\).
Step 2. Upfront \(= (s-c)\times RPV01 = 0.0200 \times 4.106 = 0.0821\), i.e. 8.21 points paid by the protection buyer, excluding accrued.
Step 3. On \$10m notional: \(8.21\% \times 10\text{m} = \$821\text{k}\), plus accrued on the premium from the last coupon date.
Step 4 (sanity). Rule of thumb: each 1bp of running spread gap is about 0.041 points at this RPV01. Paying 100bp running on a name worth 300bp means the buyer is underpaying by 200bp a year for about 4.1 years of effective duration, so about 8 points.
Step 5 (check). At a 500bp coupon, \(U = (0.03-0.05)\times4.106 = -8.21\) points: the seller pays the buyer 8.21 points. The coupon is a convention; the economic value is the same up to the coupon-to-upfront mapping.

front: Case study: You buy 10m of 5y protection at 100bp (RPV01 about 4.46). After one month the 4y-11m point, linearly interpolated between 4y at 90bp and 5y at 100bp, is 99.2bp (RPV01 about 4.39). Compute the one-month carry and roll.
back:
Step 1 (carry). Premium paid: \(10\text{m} \times 1\% / 12 = \$8{,}333\) (cash outflow for the protection buyer).
Step 2 (roll-down). The position is marked as (spread at remaining tenor minus contract coupon) times RPV01: \((0.0099167 - 0.0100) \times 4.39 \times 10\text{m} = -\$3{,}661\). Roll-down costs the buyer because the curve slopes up.
Step 3 (total). \(-8{,}333 - 3{,}661 \approx -\$12.0\text{k}\) per month,.
Step 4 (sanity). Annual carry of 100bp on 10m is \$100k. The roll adds about 0.8bp of spread drift per month on a 10bp per year slope. Carry dominates unless the slope is steep.
Interviewer follow-up: What makes it a roll cost rather than a curve move? The position itself gets shorter, so the spread it is marked at moves along the curve even with no market move.

front: Case study: Single name at 150bp (5y RPV01 4.3) is hedged with iTraxx Main at 70bp (RPV01 4.5). Name notional 10m. Spread beta is 1.6 in percentage terms. Size the index hedge and check the P&L for a 10bp index widening.
back:
Step 1 (bp beta). Percent beta \(\beta=1.6\) means \(\%\Delta S_n = 1.6\times\%\Delta S_I\). A 1bp index move is \(1/70 = 1.43\%\), so the name moves \(1.6\times 1.43\% \times 150 = 3.43\)bp. The bp beta is \(\beta S_n/S_I = 3.43\).
Step 2 (notional). Name CS01 \(= 10\text{m}\times 4.3\times 10^{-4} = \$4{,}300\) per bp. Index hedge notional \(N_I\) with CS01 \(N_I \times 4.5\times 10^{-4}\) must equal \(3.43\times\$4{,}300 = \$14{,}750\) per index bp, so \(N_I = \$32.8\)m.
Step 3 (P&L check). A 10bp index widening gives the name +34.3bp: long-protection P&L \(\approx 10\text{m}\times 4.3\times 0.00343 = \$147\text{k}\). The index sold leg loses \(32.8\text{m}\times4.5\times 0.0010 = \$147\text{k}\). Net zero to first order.
Step 4 (sanity). A 2.1x notional ratio on the index looks large but comes from the 150/70 spread ratio times beta 1.6, which is the economic point: a high-spread name is much more index-sensitive in bp.
Where it breaks: beta is estimated and unstable; the name-specific move is not captured; the hedge is delta-only and does not cover the name's idiosyncratic jump.

front: Case study: Negative basis trade on 10m: bond bought at par with ASW 150bp; 5y CDS protection bought at 120bp; carry 30bp. Default happens at year 2. Recovery on the bond is 35; the CDS auction settles at 40 (assume the bond is not a deliverable in the auction, so the auction price is not capped by it). Compute the P&L across default with and without the recovery mismatch.
back:
Step 1 (carry to default). \(10\text{m}\times 0.30\% \times 2 = \$60\text{k}\).
Step 2 (case with matching recovery at 35). Bond recovers \(3.5\text{m}\). CDS pays \((1-0.35)\times 10\text{m} = 6.5\text{m}\). Principal flow: \(3.5 + 6.5 - 10 = 0\). Total P&L = \$60k carry.
Step 3 (mismatch at auction 40). CDS pays \((1-0.40)\times 10\text{m} = 6.0\text{m}\). Principal flow: \(3.5 + 6.0 - 10 = -0.5\text{m}\). Total P&L = \(60\text{k} - 500\text{k} = -\$440\text{k}\).
Step 4 (sanity). The mismatch equals the difference in recovery times notional: \(0.05\times 10\text{m} = \$500\text{k}\). Carry of \$60k is about 1/8 of the loss; a 5-point auction-versus-bond difference wipes out about 17 years of carry at 30bp on 10m.
Interviewer follow-up: What is the asset-swap unwind at default? It is a separate cash flow and depends on the swap's terms; it is omitted here, so the result is the principal-plus-carry P&L only.

front: Case study: A 5s10s steepener on one issuer: 5y protection at 120bp (RPV01 4.42), 10y protection at 150bp (RPV01 7.69), recovery 40%. Size the trade JTD-neutral and compute its carry, CS01 and the P&L of a 10bp parallel widening. Then compare with CS01-neutral sizing.
back:
Step 1 (JTD-neutral). Buy 10y protection and sell 5y protection, both at par at inception. JTD = \(N(1-R)\) per leg, so \(N_{10} = N_5\). Take \(N_5 = N_{10} = 10\text{m}\); net JTD = 0.
Step 2 (carry). Pay \(1.50\%\times 10\text{m} = \$150\text{k}\), receive \(1.20\%\times 10\text{m} = \$120\text{k}\). Carry = \(-\$30\text{k}\) per year, \(-\$2.5\text{k}\) per month.
Step 3 (CS01). 5y: \(10\text{m}\times 4.42\times10^{-4} = \$4{,}420\)/bp. 10y: \(10\text{m}\times 7.69\times10^{-4} = \$7{,}690\)/bp. Net long-10y CS01 is \(\$3{,}270\)/bp.
Step 4 (parallel +10bp). P&L = \(+10\times 3{,}270 = +\$32.7\text{k}\). The JTD-neutral trade is not a spread-neutral trade; it is long the 10y.
Step 5 (CS01-neutral alternative). \(N_{10} = N_5\times 4.42/7.69 = 0.575\,N_5 = 5.75\)m. Carry becomes \(+\$120\text{k} - 1.50\%\times 5.75\text{m} = +\$34\text{k}\) per year, but net JTD = \(0.6\times(5.75 - 10) = -\$2.55\)m, i.e. a short-default position.
Interviewer follow-up: Which to choose? If you are trading the curve shape and want to be default-neutral, JTD-neutral with negative carry. If you want spread-neutral carry, accept a -\$2.55m default exposure.

front: For a flat hazard \(\lambda\) and continuous premium accrual, the par CDS spread is exactly \(\{{c1::\lambda(1-R)\}}\), and the risk-free rate {{c2::cancels}} out of the ratio.
back: Derived in the flat-hazard par derivation card. Discrete quarterly premiums with accrued-on-default move the 5y par by about 1bp at \(\lambda=5\%\) (301.1bp vs 300.0bp).

front: Under the ISDA standard model the upfront of a CDS with par spread \(s\) and coupon \(c\) is {{c1::\((s-c)\times RPV01\)}}, and the protection buyer {{c2::pays}} it when \(s > c\).
back: Plus accrued premium from the last coupon date (ACT/360) paid in cash. Sign flips when the coupon is above the par spread (the seller pays the buyer).

front: For a homogeneous pool of \(N\) names with common hazard \(\lambda\), the first default has intensity {{c1::\(N\lambda\)}}, so the front-end protection on a knockout index option is approximately {{c2::\((1-R)/N\)}} of index notional when \(N\lambda T\) is large.
back: With \(N=125\), \(\lambda=5\%\), \(R=40\%\): \((1-R)/N = 0.48\%\). For a 1y expiry the FEP is about 0.477%, and the probability that no default occurs is about 0.2%, so the option is almost pure FEP.

front: A protection buyer's jump-to-default P&L is {{c1::\(N(1-R) - V\)}}, where \(V\) is the {{c2::mark-to-market to the holder}} of the contract just before default.
back: The \(-V\) term is the trap: a book that is "JTD-neutral" at inception is not JTD-neutral after the legs move. For a 10y leg with \(V = \$77\)k the JTD is \$5.92m rather than \$6.00m.

front: In the large-pool limit of the one-factor Gaussian copula the conditional loss given market factor \(M\) is {{c1::\((1-R)\,\Phi\big((\Phi^{-1}(p)-\sqrt{\rho}M)/\sqrt{1-\rho}\big)\)}}, and the tranche EL is the expectation of the tranche payoff divided by {{c2::\(B-A\)}}.
back: Pool EL \((1-R)p\) at \(M\) integrated gives the unconditional loss. The tranche EL is non-monotone in \(\rho\) for mezzanine tranches, which is why base correlation is used.
